rv.q: “Kowalski” neatly sidesteps the largest trap lying in wait, because neither Taylor nor Flynn is doing an impersonation.
Kowalski is an intelligent entertainment, joyously steeped in history.
Kowalski presents us with a fascinating glimpse of two of the theater’s most celebrated icons.

Gregg Ostrin’s Kowalski is both entertaining and revealing, dramatizing Tennessee Williams at the height and Marlon Brando on the verge of his great success and the theater references are exactly right for the period.
A playful and highly watchable tribute to both Williams and Brando, it has some surprisingly astute things to say about the tectonic cultural shifts happening in our own time.
Through two sparkling performances, Tennessee Williams and Marlon Brando come to life again.
Kowalski would be a much stronger play if the tug-of-war we witness between Williams and Brando were on more of an equal footing.

Yet, I do think the distortions matter, not just because they do an injustice to the memory of these two talented artists, but because in this way “Kowalski” becomes self-sabotaging, undermining a well-designed, well-acted production, and especially the charismatic performance of Brando by Brandon Flynn.
Kowalski is based on a true event; unfortunately, very little about it rings true.

Playwright Gregg Ostrin has done his research -- Kowalski is dotted with comments about actors, critics, and some of Williams' theatrical misadventures -- but the result is a slick, uninspired exercise, a Vanity Fair article without the juicy, gossipy amusement.
Ultimately, Kowalski is a fascinating exploration of two extraordinary minds colliding in a moment that would change theater forever.
Ostrin, Hanlon, and the cast deliver both the entertainment and the insights.
The new play hits all the right dance moves, and ends at precisely the right moment after the perfectly delivered line.
Ostrin finds a surprising and hilarious solution to the problem, featuring a dead-on delivery by Flynn and a silent reaction by Taylor that speaks volumes.
You only have two months to catch this electric iteration of Cabaret at The Kit Kat Club...
Kowalski offers a vision of the past that strays far from the shadows of the real, but ultimately settles for legerdemain rather than pure magic.

cn.t: Critics find this fictionalized account of Tennessee Williams and Marlon Brando's first meeting mostly engaging, praising the performances and intriguing premise, though some cite a clunky script and questionable fabrications.
